cues.text: Welcome to Equilibrium.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Equilibrium is dynamic: opposing changes continue at equal, nonzero rates.
Imagine liquid water in a closed container at fixed temperature.
Water evaporates while vapour condenses.
At equilibrium the amounts remain constant because the two rates balance, not
because the molecules stop moving.
Equal rates do not require equal amounts.
Similar reasoning applies to melting and freezing, sublimation and deposition,
and reversible chemical reactions.
The conditions and phases must be specified.
For a gas dissolved in a liquid, one common Henry law convention is gas
partial
pressure equals Henry's constant times the dissolved gas mole fraction.
At fixed temperature and pressure, a larger constant in this convention means
a
smaller dissolved mole fraction.
Suppose the gas partial pressure is two bar and the constant is one thousand
bar.
Divide two by one thousand to obtain mole fraction zero point zero zero two.
Doubling the partial pressure doubles that mole fraction within the dilute
model.
A different convention can put the concentration on the other side, so do not
compare constants before checking definitions.
This distinction between a changing rate and a fixed equilibrium composition
will guide the remaining chapters.
The reaction quotient Q describes the present mixture.
The equilibrium constant K describes equilibrium at the specified temperature.
For a balanced reaction, multiply product activities raised to their
coefficients and divide by the corresponding reactant product.
Pure solids and pure liquids have unit activity in their reference states and
are omitted from the usual expression.
If Q is smaller than K, the forward direction is favoured; if larger, the
reverse direction is favoured.
Consider hydrogen plus iodine forming two hydrogen iodide molecules, all
gases.
In the ideal concentration convention, Q is hydrogen iodide concentration
squared divided by hydrogen concentration times iodine concentration.
Let those concentrations be zero point two zero, zero point one zero, and zero
point one zero molar respectively.
Q is four.
If K is fifty at that temperature, the mixture proceeds forward.
Reversing a reaction replaces K with its reciprocal.
Doubling every coefficient squares K.
For conventional ideal gas expressions, K p equals K c times R T raised to
the gaseous mole change.
In this example, two gas molecules replace two gas molecules, so the exponent
is zero.
Keep the pressure, concentration and gas constant conventions consistent.
Rigorous thermodynamic equilibrium constants are dimensionless and use
activities relative to reference states.
Le Chatelier's principle helps predict a response, but checking Q is more
reliable than memorizing slogans.
For nitrogen plus three hydrogen forming two ammonia molecules, compression at
unchanged temperature increases all reacting ideal gas partial pressures.
The denominator in Q has total power four, while the numerator has power two.
If all partial pressures double, Q falls by a factor of four.
Starting at equilibrium, Q is then below K, so formation of ammonia is
favoured.
Compression does not change K at fixed temperature.
Adding an inert ideal gas at fixed volume leaves the reacting gases' partial
pressures unchanged, so it causes no shift in this model.
At fixed total pressure the volume increases, and the outcome can differ.
Heating changes K and favours the endothermic direction.
For an exothermic forward reaction, heating favours the reverse direction.
A catalyst accelerates the approach to equilibrium without changing its
composition or K at the same temperature.
Removing a product can favour further product formation, provided the relevant
phase and activity actually change.
Adding more of a pure solid already present does not simply multiply its
activity.
State the temperature, volume or pressure constraint.
An acid can be described in several ways.
An Arrhenius acid increases hydrogen ion concentration in water.
A Bronsted acid donates a proton, and a Bronsted base accepts one.
A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.
A conjugate acid and base differ by one proton.
Ammonia and ammonium are one such pair.
Acid strength refers to ionization behaviour, while concentration describes
how
much acid is present.
Do not infer pH from the word strong alone.
Strictly, pH is minus the base ten logarithm of hydrogen ion activity.
In an elementary dilute model we use the numerical molar concentration.
At twenty five degrees Celsius, the water ion product is approximately ten to
the minus fourteen.
The sum of pH and pOH is then approximately fourteen.
A hydrogen ion concentration of ten to the minus three molar gives pH three.
A hydroxide concentration of ten to the minus five molar gives pOH five and pH
nine at this temperature.
Neutrality means equal hydrogen and hydroxide activities, not an unconditional
pH of seven at every temperature.
Extremely dilute acid solutions require water ionization to be included; a
strong acid concentration of ten to the minus eight molar cannot simply be
assigned pH eight.
For a monoprotic weak acid, let the initial concentration be C and the
dissociated amount be x.
Ignoring water ionization, the acid constant equals x squared divided by C
minus x.
If x is much smaller than C, replacing the denominator by C gives x
approximately the square root of the acid constant times C.
With C equal to zero point one zero zero molar and the acid constant ten to
the
minus five, x is approximately zero point zero zero one zero zero molar.
The pH is about three, and only one percent dissociates.
That small fraction supports the approximation.
Now take both C and the acid constant as zero point zero zero one zero zero.
The shortcut predicts complete dissociation, contradicting its own assumption.
Solve the quadratic instead.
The positive root is minus the acid constant plus the square root of its
square
plus four times the acid constant times C, all divided by two.
The result is about zero point zero zero zero six one eight molar, giving pH
three point two zero nine.
About sixty two percent dissociates.
The example shows why weak does not automatically mean slightly dissociated at
every dilution.
Check both the neglected dissociation fraction and whether water's own ions
matter.
A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in useful amounts.
The acid consumes added base, while the conjugate base consumes added acid.
First complete the strong acid or base reaction using moles.
Only then apply the Henderson Hasselbalch approximation: pH equals p K a plus
the base ten logarithm of remaining conjugate base divided by remaining acid.
Suppose the buffer contains twenty millimoles of acid and thirty millimoles of
conjugate base.
Add five millimoles of strong acid.
It consumes five millimoles of conjugate base and forms five millimoles of
weak
acid, leaving twenty five millimoles of each.
Their concentration ratio equals their mole ratio because they share the same
final volume.
The ratio is one, so with p K a four point seven six, the final pH is
approximately four point seven six.
Using the original thirty over twenty ratio would ignore the neutralization.
A ten to one base to acid ratio would instead add one pH unit.
Diluting both partners equally initially preserves their ratio approximately,
but reduces buffer capacity.
If one partner is exhausted, stop using the two partner buffer formula and
account for excess strong reagent and any relevant hydrolysis.
Salt solutions need not be neutral.
Acetate accepts a proton from water and produces hydroxide, so sodium acetate
is basic in the elementary aqueous model.
Ammonium can donate a proton to water, so ammonium chloride is acidic.
Sodium and chloride are spectators here.
For a conjugate pair at a given temperature, the acid constant times the base
constant equals the water ion product.
Consider zero point one zero zero molar sodium acetate at twenty five degrees
Celsius.
If the acetic acid constant is ten to the minus five, acetate's base constant
is ten to the minus nine.
The small hydrolysis estimate gives hydroxide concentration equal to the
square
root of the base constant times concentration, or ten to the minus five molar.
The pOH is five and the pH is nine.
Only zero point zero one percent of the acetate hydrolyses, so replacing its
remaining concentration by the starting value is justified.
The hydroxide concentration is also large compared with the neutral water
background in this example.
A salt of a strong acid and strong base is approximately neutral when neither
ion hydrolyses appreciably.
Salts with two reacting ions, amphiprotic species and very dilute solutions
need additional equilibrium analysis.
Identify the reacting ion before choosing a shortcut.
Solubility products depend on stoichiometry.
Silver chloride produces one silver ion and one chloride ion, so its dilute
ion
product is their concentration product.
In pure water, molar solubility s gives a product of s squared.
If an illustrative solubility product is ten to the minus ten, the solubility
is ten to the minus five molar.
With zero point zero one zero molar background chloride and no competing
reactions, the approximate solubility falls to ten to the minus eight molar.
Check that this is small compared with the background.
A salt producing one A ion and two B ions instead gives four times s cubed.
Mixing requires dilution before comparing the ion product with the solubility
product.
Mix equal volumes of silver and chloride stock solutions, each two times ten
to
the minus five molar.
Each concentration halves, so the initial ion product is ten to the minus ten.
With the illustrative constant above, this is exactly the saturation boundary,
not supersaturation.
A larger ion product permits precipitation; a smaller one permits more
dissolution if solid is available.
Common ions usually reduce solubility, but complex formation and acid base
reactions can modify the result.
Use the seven worked examples and twelve original questions in the notes to
practise these checks.
Pressure and concentration equilibrium expressions must use compatible
conventions.
For an ideal gas, partial pressure equals concentration times R T.
If the pressure quotient uses each pressure divided by its standard pressure
and the concentration quotient uses each concentration divided by its standard
concentration, their conversion includes R T times standard concentration
divided by standard pressure.
Raise that dimensionless factor to the gaseous product mole count minus the
gaseous reactant mole count.
For dinitrogen tetroxide forming two nitrogen dioxide molecules, the change is
one.
Take standard concentration one mole per litre, standard pressure one bar,
temperature three hundred kelvin and R zero point zero eight three one four
litre bar per mole kelvin.
The conversion factor is twenty four point nine four two.
A supplied concentration based constant of zero point one zero zero therefore
corresponds to a pressure based constant about two point four nine four under
these conventions.
When the gaseous mole change is zero, the factor cancels.
Count gaseous species only and state the standards rather than silently
combining incompatible units or treating every reported constant as the same
numerical quantity.
Gas dissociation changes the total number of molecules, so the reacted
fraction
is not generally the same as the product mole fraction.
Begin with one mole of pure dinitrogen tetroxide.
If a fraction alpha dissociates, one minus alpha mole remains and two alpha
moles of nitrogen dioxide form.
The total is one plus alpha.
At twenty percent dissociation, the amounts are zero point eight and zero
point
four mole, with a total of one point two.
The nitrogen dioxide mole fraction is therefore one third and the tetroxide
fraction two thirds.
At total pressure one bar, their partial pressures are one third bar and two
thirds bar.
With standard pressure one bar, the dimensionless pressure quotient is the
square of one third divided by two thirds, giving one sixth.
The general expression contains four alpha squared divided by one minus alpha
squared, multiplied by total pressure divided by standard pressure.
Check both atom balance and total moles before inserting a pressure.
This model starts with pure reactant and assumes ideal gases without an inert
gas or another competing reaction.
In a strong acid strong base titration, calculate the neutralization amounts
before the remaining ion concentration.
Start with twenty five millilitres of zero point one zero zero molar
hydrochloric acid.
It contains zero point zero zero two five zero mole of acid.
Adding twenty millilitres of equally concentrated sodium hydroxide consumes
zero point zero zero two zero zero mole, leaving zero point zero zero zero
five
zero mole of hydrogen ions in forty five millilitres.
The concentration is about zero point zero one one one molar and p H about one
point nine five.
At twenty five millilitres of base, the stoichiometric amounts are equal.
For this ideal strong acid strong base example at twenty five degrees Celsius,
p H is approximately seven.
At thirty millilitres, excess hydroxide is zero point zero zero zero five zero
mole in fifty five millilitres, giving p O H about two point zero four and p H
about eleven point nine six.
Total volume matters on both sides of equivalence.
A weak acid titration has different equilibrium behaviour, so do not transfer
the neutral equivalence conclusion to every acid base pair.
A solubility product constrains free ion activities, not the total amount of
every metal containing species in solution.
For a simple dilute silver chloride model, use the concentration product as an
approximation to the activity expression.
With illustrative solubility product one point eight times ten to the minus
ten, pure water gives equal silver and chloride concentrations and a molar
solubility about one point three four times ten to the minus five.
Now suppose the solution already contains zero point zero one zero molar
chloride.
If additional dissolution is small, free chloride remains approximately that
value.
Divide the solubility product by zero point zero one zero to obtain silver
concentration one point eight times ten to the minus eight molar.
The added dissolution is tiny relative to the initial chloride, so the
approximation is self consistent.
This common ion lowers simple solubility in the stated model.
Complex formation, other equilibria and nonideal activities can alter the
result.
In particular, total dissolved silver need not equal free silver when
complexes
are important.
Check what concentration the question actually asks for before applying the
product expression.
An amphiprotic species can accept or donate a proton.
Hydrogen carbonate is a familiar intermediate in a diprotic acid system.
Its acid behaviour is controlled by the second acid dissociation constant,
while its base behaviour is related to the first constant through the water
ion
product.
Under the appropriate intermediate salt approximation, p H is approximately
half the sum of the two p K a values.
For illustrative values six point three and ten point three, the estimate is
eight point three.
This is a mildly basic result even though the formula contains hydrogen.
Do not classify a salt as acidic simply because its anion still carries a
proton.
The average formula assumes conditions where the amphiprotic salt contribution
dominates water effects and the approximations used in its derivation are
adequate.
Very dilute solutions, additional acids or bases, and important competing
equilibria can require a fuller mass and charge balance.
The two constants must refer to the same acid system, solvent and temperature.
A useful answer states the model and its limits alongside the numerical
average.
An equilibrium constant belongs to a balanced reaction at a stated
temperature.
Changing the equation changes the corresponding constant.
Suppose the supplied dimensionless constant for nitrogen plus three hydrogen
forming two ammonia molecules is sixteen.
Reversing that equation inverts the reaction quotient, so the reverse constant
is one sixteenth.
Halving every coefficient takes the square root, giving four for half nitrogen
plus three halves hydrogen forming one ammonia.
Reversing and then halving gives one quarter, not one eighth.
Adding two reactions multiplies their constants because the corresponding
quotients multiply and any common intermediate activities cancel.
For a supplied reaction converting X to Y with constant five, followed by Y to
Z with constant four, the net X to Z constant is twenty.
These operations use the same temperature and compatible standard state
conventions.
The constant is not multiplied by two merely because every reaction
coefficient
was doubled.
Write the transformed quotient or combine standard Gibbs energies if unsure.
These bookkeeping rules do not supply the new constant at another temperature;
temperature dependence requires additional thermodynamic information.
A pure solid does not appear as a variable concentration factor in the usual
equilibrium expression while that pure phase is present.
Consider calcium carbonate solid reversibly forming calcium oxide solid and
carbon dioxide gas at a fixed temperature.
If both pure solid phases coexist, their activities are one in the chosen
standard states, and the dimensionless equilibrium constant is carbon dioxide
partial pressure divided by standard pressure.
Suppose the supplied constant is zero point two zero zero and standard
pressure
is one bar.
The equilibrium carbon dioxide pressure is then zero point two zero zero bar.
Adding more calcium carbonate alone does not raise that equilibrium pressure
when both solids remain present.
Compressing the gas volume initially raises its carbon dioxide pressure;
reaction can then proceed in the reverse direction until the equilibrium
pressure is restored, provided enough appropriate solid remains.
Adding an inert gas at fixed volume leaves carbon dioxide partial pressure
unchanged in an ideal gas mixture, even though total pressure rises.
If a solid phase is exhausted or the temperature changes, the simple
coexistence pressure conclusion must be reconsidered.
Identify partial pressure and phase presence before using a shortcut.
A weak base calculation should check whether its ionization is small enough
for
a square root approximation.
Take an uncharged base in water with supplied concentration zero point zero
zero one zero zero molar and base constant one times ten to the minus four.
Assume ideal dilute behaviour and neglect water autoionization relative to the
hydroxide produced.
Let x be the equilibrium hydroxide concentration.
The conjugate acid concentration is also x, while unreacted base is C minus x.
The base constant is x squared divided by C minus x.
Solving the quadratic gives approximately zero point zero zero zero two seven
zero molar hydroxide.
This is about twenty seven percent of the initial base concentration, so
replacing C minus x by C is not justified.
The square root estimate would be zero point zero zero zero three one six
molar, noticeably higher.
Using the quadratic value gives p O H about three point five seven and, with
supplied p K w fourteen at twenty five degrees Celsius, p H about ten point
four three.
The subtraction from fourteen is temperature dependent through the ionic
product of water.
A very dilute base may require including water ionization as well.
Selective precipitation begins with comparing ion products, not simply
choosing
the smaller printed solubility constant without regard to composition.
Consider two hypothetical one to one salts, A X and B X, whose cations are
each
initially zero point zero one zero zero molar after any mixing dilution.
Their supplied solubility products are one times ten to the minus ten and one
times ten to the minus eight.
Assume ideal behaviour, no complexation and negligible volume change while
adding the common anion X.
The onset anion concentrations are one times ten to the minus eight molar for
A
X and one times ten to the minus six for B X.
Thus A X begins precipitating first.
Just as B X reaches its onset, the remaining dissolved A concentration set by
A
X saturation is one times ten to the minus four molar.
Relative to the original zero point zero one zero zero, ninety nine percent of
A has been removed.
Equality of ion product and constant marks saturation, not an already large
precipitate amount.
For different stoichiometries, unequal starting concentrations or significant
dilution, recalculate the full expressions before predicting separation
quality.
Very dilute strong acid solutions require water's own ions in the balance.
Consider an ideal aqueous model at twenty five degrees Celsius with water ion
product ten to the minus fourteen and fully dissociated monoprotic acid
concentration ten to the minus eight molar.
Ignoring water would predict p H eight, incorrectly making added acid appear
basic.
Let H denote the total hydrogen ion concentration.
Charge balance gives H equal to the acid anion concentration plus hydroxide
concentration.
Substituting hydroxide equal to K w divided by H produces the quadratic H
squared minus C H minus K w equal to zero.
Its positive root is about one point zero five one two five times ten to the
minus seven molar, giving p H six point nine seven eight.
The value is slightly acidic and approaches seven from below as the added acid
concentration approaches zero.
This calculation assumes ideal activities, complete acid dissociation and no
other acid base species.
Dissolved carbon dioxide or impurities can matter greatly at such low
concentrations.
A mathematical concentration example is not a claim that an unprotected
laboratory sample automatically meets those assumptions.
The ionized fraction of a weak acid and its hydrogen ion concentration are
different measures.
Compare two separate solutions of the same monoprotic acid at the same
temperature, with supplied acid constant ten to the minus five.
Their formal concentrations are zero point one zero zero molar and zero point
zero zero one zero zero molar.
Ignoring water ionization, solve the same exact weak acid quadratic for each
concentration.
The more concentrated solution has hydrogen ion concentration about nine point
nine five zero times ten to the minus four molar and ionized fraction about
zero point nine nine five percent.
The dilute solution has hydrogen ion concentration about nine point five one
two times ten to the minus five molar and ionized fraction about nine point
five one percent.
Thus dilution raises the fraction ionized while lowering the hydrogen ion
concentration.
The p H rises from about three point zero zero two to four point zero two two.
The acid constant stays unchanged at fixed temperature in this model.
Avoid describing the diluted acid as intrinsically stronger simply because a
larger fraction ionizes.
At still greater dilution, include water's ions.
A solubility product must use both the correct ion coefficients and their
powers.
Consider a hypothetical sparingly soluble solid with formula A two B three,
where the ions are A three plus and B two minus.
One formula unit dissolves into two A ions and three B ions, conserving both
atoms and total charge.
If its molar solubility in pure water is s, the free ion concentrations are
two
s and three s in the stated ideal model.
The concentration product is two s squared times three s cubed, or one hundred
eight times s to the fifth power.
For supplied product constant one point zero eight times ten to the minus
eighteen, the molar solubility is ten to the minus four molar.
The A and B ion concentrations are therefore two and three times ten to the
minus four molar.
Taking a square root of the constant would use the wrong stoichiometry.
This numerical model excludes hydrolysis, ion pairing, complexation and
additional common ions.
Actual multivalent salts often require those effects, so retain the explicit
assumptions rather than treating the expression as a complete real salt
analysis.
A metal hydroxide precipitation threshold combines solubility with water's
acid
base balance.
Use an ideal hypothetical divalent metal model with supplied hydroxide
solubility product ten to the minus eleven.
The free metal concentration before precipitation is zero point zero one zero
zero molar.
Saturation requires hydroxide concentration equal to the square root of K s p
divided by metal concentration, giving three point one six two times ten to
the
minus five molar.
At twenty five degrees Celsius with p K w fourteen, this is p O H four point
five and p H nine point five.
Equality marks the saturation boundary; it does not imply a large amount has
already precipitated.
Now hold the solution at p H ten with negligible volume change.
Hydroxide is ten to the minus four molar, so saturated free metal
concentration
is zero point zero zero one zero zero molar.
Relative to the original amount, ninety percent is removed in this simplified
model.
Complexation, amphoteric redissolution, hydrolysis and other solids are
excluded.
The p H must be maintained; hydroxide consumed by precipitation can otherwise
change it.
A salt can contain both an acidic cation and a basic anion.
Let the cation be B H plus, conjugate to weak base B, and the anion be A
minus,
conjugate to weak acid H A.
Their reactions with water compete; neither ion should automatically be called
a spectator.
For a moderately concentrated ideal solution with small hydrolysis and water
background negligible in the charge balance, the approximate p H is half of p
K
w plus p K a of H A minus p K b of B.
Use a supplied zero point one zero molar salt at twenty five degrees Celsius,
acid constant ten to the minus five and original base constant ten to the
minus
four.
The p H estimate is seven point five, so the salt is mildly basic.
The cation's acid constant is ten to the minus ten and the anion's base
constant ten to the minus nine, consistent with the stronger basic
contribution.
This formula compares the parent acid and base, not two unrelated constants.
At extreme dilution or extensive hydrolysis, solve mass balance, charge
balance
and water ionization together instead of claiming that concentration never
matters.
A diprotic acid can show two successive neutralization stages when its acid
constants are well separated.
Consider zero point zero one zero zero mole of a hypothetical acid H two A,
with supplied p K a values four and nine, titrated by a strong base.
At zero point zero zero five zero zero mole of added hydroxide, the first
buffer pair contains approximately equal amounts of H two A and H A minus.
Its p H is therefore approximately four.
The first stoichiometric equivalence is at zero point zero one zero zero mole
hydroxide, where H A minus predominates and can either accept or donate a
proton.
In the usual amphiprotic approximation its p H is half of four plus nine, or
six point five.
At zero point zero one five zero mole hydroxide, the second buffer pair, H A
minus and A two minus, has equal amounts, giving p H approximately nine.
Full neutralization requires zero point zero two zero zero mole hydroxide, not
the first equivalence amount.
These are well separated equilibrium approximations at suitable concentration,
not exact values for arbitrary dilution.
Past the second equivalence, calculate excess hydroxide and total volume
before
p H.
Mixing acid solutions does not mean averaging their p H values.
Consider two distinct monoprotic weak acids whose analytical concentrations
after mixing are each zero point one zero molar.
Their supplied acid constants are ten to the minus five and four times ten to
the minus five.
Both acids establish equilibrium with the same hydrogen ion concentration.
Each conjugate base concentration is its analytical concentration times its
acid constant, divided by hydrogen ion concentration plus that acid constant.
Charge balance adds those two anion concentrations and hydroxide to match
hydrogen ions.
If dissociation is small and hydrogen ions dominate water's contribution,
hydrogen concentration squared is approximately the sum of acid constant times
concentration for both acids.
The sum here is five times ten to the minus six, giving hydrogen ions about
two
point two four times ten to the minus three molar and p H approximately two
point six five.
Check that each acid constant is small compared with this hydrogen
concentration before trusting that shortcut.
An exact ideal charge balance gives a nearby result.
The common hydrogen ions suppress the individual dissociation fractions;
neither isolated acid's p H can simply be added or averaged into the mixture
answer.
A soluble complex can increase a sparingly soluble salt's total dissolved
amount while free metal ions remain scarce.
Use a supplied ideal silver chloride model with solubility product ten to the
minus ten and formation constant ten to the seven for the diamminesilver ion.
Hold the free ammonia concentration at zero point one zero molar, neglecting
other complexes and reactions.
If s is total dissolved silver and no chloride was initially added, chloride
concentration also equals s.
Free silver is only s divided by one plus formation constant times free
ammonia
squared.
Substituting into the solubility product gives s squared equal to ten to the
minus ten times one hundred thousand and one.
Thus total solubility is approximately zero point zero zero three one six
molar, while free silver is approximately three point one six times ten to the
minus eight molar.
Multiplying dissolution and complex formation constants also gives the overall
reaction constant.
The ligand concentration in these expressions is free ammonia, not the amount
initially poured in.
Bound ammonia consumes almost two ligand units per dissolved silver here, so
maintaining the stipulated free concentration requires an adequate ligand
inventory.
Adding an inert gas changes total pressure without necessarily changing the
reacting gases' partial pressures.
Consider an ideal equilibrium of dinitrogen tetroxide forming two nitrogen
dioxide molecules at a fixed temperature.
At fixed volume, each reacting species still has partial pressure equal to its
own mole amount times R T divided by that unchanged volume.
The extra inert gas raises total pressure, but the reaction quotient remains
at
its original equilibrium value, so there is no composition shift in this ideal
model.
Now impose fixed total pressure instead, allowing the volume to double after
inert gas addition before chemical reequilibration.
Each reacting partial pressure is initially halved.
Because the quotient has the nitrogen dioxide pressure squared divided by the
dinitrogen tetroxide pressure, it becomes half its old value.
The quotient is now below K, so dissociation proceeds forward toward the side
with more gas molecules.
K itself is unchanged because temperature is unchanged.
For a reaction with zero net gas mole change, uniform partial pressure scaling
cancels from the quotient.
Name the constraint and calculate partial pressures instead of applying a rule
based only on the words pressure increases.
Two buffers with the same conjugate base to acid ratio can begin at the same
pH
while resisting an added acid by different amounts.
Use a weak acid with p K a five and two separate one liter ideal buffer
samples.
The smaller inventory contains zero point zero one zero mole each of acid and
conjugate base.
The larger inventory contains zero point one zero zero mole each.
Both ratios start at one, giving approximate pH five.
Add zero point zero zero five mole of strong acid to each, with negligible
volume change.
Neutralization consumes conjugate base and creates weak acid before the buffer
equation is used.
The smaller sample then contains zero point zero zero five mole base and zero
point zero one five mole acid, giving approximate pH four point five two.
The larger sample has zero point zero nine five mole base and zero point one
zero five mole acid, giving about four point nine six.
The larger inventory changes pH less.
If the added acid exceeds the available conjugate base, this simple buffer
ratio calculation no longer applies; excess strong acid and remaining
equilibria must be considered.
Ratio controls the initial pH, while amounts help determine capacity.
The salt that precipitates first need not be removed completely before another
salt starts forming.
Use a stipulated constant volume ideal mixture initially containing chloride
and bromide, each at zero point zero one zero molar.
Neglect complex formation and activity effects.
Supplied solubility products are one times ten to the minus ten for silver
chloride and five times ten to the minus thirteen for silver bromide.
Silver bromide begins precipitating at the lower free silver concentration,
five times ten to the minus eleven molar.
Silver chloride begins when free silver reaches one times ten to the minus
eight molar, while chloride remains essentially at its initial concentration
up
to that onset.
With silver bromide solid present at this boundary, dissolved bromide is five
times ten to the minus five molar.
That is zero point five percent of its initial concentration, so ninety nine
point five percent has precipitated.
A requested ninety nine point nine percent bromide removal before any silver
chloride precipitation is not achievable in this supplied model.
Compare the residual amount with the stated separation target, not merely the
order of onset.
Dilution, complexes and nonideal activities would require a more complete
calculation.
An acid base indicator changes its dominant color because two chemical forms
have different colors and their ratio depends on pH.
Represent a simple indicator as a weak acid H In and its conjugate base In
minus.
In a dilute ideal comparison, the base to acid indicator ratio is ten raised
to
pH minus the indicator p K a.
With p K a nine, pH eight gives ratio one tenth, pH nine gives equal amounts,
and pH ten gives ratio ten.
The common approximate color transition interval spans a ratio from one to ten
through ten to one, corresponding to p K a minus one through plus one.
That is not a statement that every observer or indicator has identical
visibility thresholds.
When choosing an indicator for a titration, its transition should fall within
the steep pH change near the chemical equivalence point under the stated
conditions.
The observed endpoint and the stoichiometric equivalence point are related but
distinct.
An indicator is usually added in a small enough amount to avoid significantly
changing the sample equilibrium.
Its p K a is not automatically the p K a of the acid being titrated.
